title: Freelancing and Online Work Basics
summary: Learn how to choose skills, build a portfolio, write proposals, price your time, agree terms, get paid safely and avoid scams when working online.
audience: Students and young adults who want to earn from remote or online work

lessons.title: Types of remote work and choosing skills to offer

body.p: Freelancing means selling your skills to different clients for each job instead of having one employer. You are self-employed: you find the work, agree the price, deliver it and chase payment. Online work is any job you can do and deliver over the internet, so you can serve clients in your own town or in another country. This course teaches principles. Platform rules, laws and payment options differ by country, so always check the current terms and local rules yourself.

list: Freelance projects: writing, graphic design, video editing, translation, web design, bookkeeping, data entry, social-media posts. You are paid per job or per hour.
Virtual assistance: managing a client's email, calendar, research and simple admin on a regular basis.
Microtasks and online surveys: very small tasks for small payments. These are easy to start but usually pay little per hour and are not a stable income.
Remote employment: a normal job with a company, done from home. You are an employee and the employer sets the hours and pay.
Online teaching and tutoring: helping learners in school subjects, languages or music, often live over video or phone.

body.p: Notice the trade-offs. Freelance projects can pay better per hour but work is uneven. Microtasks need no experience but pay little. Employment is steadier but has fewer openings. Many people combine them: a student might tutor on weekday evenings and take a design job at weekends.

Do not choose a skill only because it sounds fashionable. Look for the overlap of three circles: something you can already do reasonably well, something people will pay for, and something you can show by example. If all three overlap, you have a service.

body.code:
Skill audit (example: a 17-year-old student)
Can do well      : Maths, English writing, Canva posters, typing fast
People pay for   : Tutoring, simple posters for shops, typing and formatting CVs
Can show samples : 3 posters made for a school club, 1 CV template
=> Services to offer first: poster design for small businesses,
   CV typing and formatting for students

body.p: Start narrow. 'I do everything' sounds weak. 'I design flyers for small shops and market stalls' is clear, and clients can remember it. You can add services later. Also list your supporting skills: reliable internet access, a charged phone or laptop, good written English, honesty and punctuality. Clients often pick the person who replies politely and delivers on time over the one with the fanciest tools.

body.tip: Write down three services you could sell, one sentence each, using the pattern 'I help [who] to [get what result]'. Example: 'I help small shops to get clear, eye-catching flyers.'

lessons.title: Building a portfolio when you have no experience

body.p: A portfolio is a small collection of your best work that proves you can do the job. Clients do not hire you because of a long speech; they hire you because they can see a result that looks like what they need. The common worry is 'I have no clients, so I have no samples.' You can solve this by creating your own proof honestly.

list: Practice projects: choose a realistic brief, such as 'a flyer for a bakery opening', and complete it as if a client had asked. Label it clearly as a practice or sample project.
Help someone you know: a family business, a church group, a school club or a neighbour's stall. Ask permission to show the result, and ask for a short written comment.
Redo and improve: take a poorly written advert or messy spreadsheet (your own or one you have permission to use) and show before and after.
Volunteer for a small, defined job for a charity or club and keep the result.

body.p: Be honest. Never present someone else's work as yours, never invent clients or reviews, and never copy a design or text you did not make. Clients can check, and a lie can end your reputation before you start. Also respect privacy: remove personal details and confidential information from your samples unless you have written permission.

body.h: What a good portfolio looks like

body.p: Three to five strong samples are better than twenty weak ones. For each sample, add a few lines: the problem, what you did, the tools you used and the result. Numbers help when they are real. For example: 'Designed a price list for a hair salon; the owner printed 50 copies and put them in the shop.' Do not claim results you cannot prove.

body.code:
PORTFOLIO ITEM (template)
Title   : Price list for a hair salon (sample for a friend's salon)
Problem : Prices were handwritten and hard to read
What I did : Typed and laid out a one-page A4 list in Canva, large clear text
Result  : Salon printed it and displays it by the door (written permission given)
Tools   : Canva, phone camera

body.p: Where to keep it? A simple online folder or a free portfolio page, a social-media page used only for your work, or a PDF of 3 to 5 pages that you can send by email. Make sure the link opens on a phone, because many clients will view it there. Put your best sample first and your contact details last. Update it every time you finish something you are proud of.

body.tip: Ask every happy helper for one sentence you may quote, such as 'Ama delivered the flyer in two days and it looked professional.' Get their permission to use their name.

lessons.title: Finding work and writing a proposal

body.p: Work comes from several places: online freelance platforms, job boards, social-media groups, local businesses, schools and word of mouth. Local clients are often easiest for a beginner because they can meet you, trust you and pay in a way you both know. Whichever route you take, you will usually need a proposal: a short message that persuades the client you understand their problem and can solve it.

body.h: The shape of a good proposal

steps: Greet the client by name and show you read the job post. Mention one specific detail from their request.
Say in one or two lines how you would solve their problem. Do not write an essay.
Show proof: link to one or two relevant samples from your portfolio.
State the price or an estimate, the delivery time, and what is included.
Ask one clear question or give a next step, such as a quick call or a sample brief.

body.code:
Hello Mr Mensah,

I saw you need a flyer for the opening of your phone-repair shop. I can design a clear A5 flyer with your logo, prices and map, ready for printing.

Here is a similar flyer I made for a hair salon: [link]. I will send a first draft within 2 days and include 2 rounds of changes.

Price: 40 currency units for the design. You print it yourself.
Could you send your logo and the three main services you want listed?

Thank you,
Ama

list: Copy-and-paste messages that say 'Dear sir/madam, I am the best'. Clients spot these at once.
Writing about yourself for four paragraphs and never mentioning their problem.
Promising anything to win the job, such as impossible deadlines or skills you do not have.
Sending messages with spelling errors. Read it aloud, or ask a friend to read it, before you send it.

body.p: Expect many replies to be silent. A reasonable beginner might send 20 well-written proposals and hear back from a few, so do not take it personally. Keep a simple list of where you applied, the date, the reply and any follow-up. Politely follow up once after a few days. Each proposal teaches you something, so adjust the next one.

body.tip: Before you send, ask: if I were the client, would this message answer 'why this person, and what happens next?' If not, rewrite it.

lessons.title: Pricing your time: hourly, fixed price and your minimum rate

body.p: New freelancers often pick a price by guessing, or by copying the lowest they see. This can leave you working long hours for too little. A better method is to work out the minimum rate you need, which is the least you can accept and still pay your bills. All amounts below use 'currency units' (CU) so you can replace them with your own money and costs.

body.code:
Personal costs you want covered   600 CU
Savings goal                       100 CU
Tools, data bundles, software       40 CU
-------------------------------------------
Net amount you need per month      740 CU

Set aside 10% of each payment for tax/fees (example figure only)
Gross earnings needed = 740 / (1 - 0.10) = 822.22 CU

body.p: The 10 percent is only an example. Tax rules, fees and reserves differ by country and platform, so find out your own figure from official sources or a qualified person. The point is to include it, because what you invoice is not what you keep.

You are not paid for every hour you work. Finding clients, writing proposals, replying to messages, learning and doing accounts are unpaid. Suppose you can work 40 hours in a week but only 40 percent is billable: 40 x 0.40 = 16 hours. Be honest and, if you are a student with limited time, use your real figure. In our example you can bill 15 hours a week for 4 weeks = 60 billable hours per month.

body.code:
Minimum rate = gross needed / billable hours
               = 822.22 / 60
               = 13.70 CU per hour (round up to 14)

Check: 14 x 60 = 840 CU; 10% set aside = 84; you keep 756 (target was 740)

body.p: If you used the net figure only, 740 / 60 = 12.33, which would leave you short once the reserve is removed. Charging 14 CU per hour is therefore your floor. Your real price can be higher, depending on skill and market, but never lower for long.

Hourly pricing is safest when the work is unclear, because you are paid for each hour. Fixed pricing suits clear jobs, and clients like knowing the total. To set a fixed price, estimate the hours, multiply by your rate and add a buffer. Example: 12 hours x 12 CU = 144; a 25 percent buffer adds 36, so the fixed price is 180 CU. The danger is underestimating. If the job took 16 hours, your real rate is 180 / 16 = 11.25 CU per hour, below your plan. Always write down exactly what is included, and charge extra for added work.

body.tip: Track your time on every job in a notebook or phone notes. After five jobs you will know how long things really take, and your estimates will improve.

lessons.title: Agreements, contracts and getting paid safely

body.p: A written agreement is a record of what you and the client expect. It protects both sides. It does not need to be a long legal document for small jobs, but for bigger jobs you may want a proper contract. This course gives general principles only, not legal advice. Laws about contracts and payments differ by place, so check local rules and ask a qualified person for important or high-value work.

list: Scope: exactly what you will deliver, in what format.
Price: total price, currency, and whether any costs are extra.
Deadline: delivery dates and what you need from the client and by when.
Revisions: how many rounds of changes are included, and the price for more.
Payment: amounts, due dates, method, and what happens if payment is late.
Ownership: who owns the finished work and whether you may show it in your portfolio.
Ending the job: how either side can stop and how work already done is paid for.

body.code:
AGREEMENT (short form)
Job      : 1 logo, delivered as PNG and PDF
Price    : 120 CU
Payment  : 30% before start (36), 40% at first draft (48), 30% at final delivery (36)
Deadline : first draft in 5 days after deposit; final in 3 days after feedback
Changes  : 2 rounds included; extra rounds 10 CU each
Ownership: client owns the final logo after full payment
Agreed by: both parties in writing (message or email counts as a record)

body.p: Check the milestone arithmetic: 30 percent of 120 is 36, 40 percent is 48 and 30 percent is 36. 36 + 48 + 36 = 120. After the first two payments you have received 84 CU, and 36 CU remains due on delivery.

list: Use payment methods that give a record: platform escrow, bank transfer, or a well-known mobile-money service that is available to both of you. Always read the terms and fees of the method you use, because they change.
Ask for a deposit on larger jobs, and split big jobs into milestones so you are never far ahead of what you have been paid.
Do not send the final, unwatermarked files until payment has cleared, not just until a screenshot shows it was 'sent'.
If you work through a platform, keep communication and payment inside it. Moving off-platform may break its rules and remove your protection.
Send a clear invoice with the job description, amount, date and payment details, and keep a copy.

body.p: Fees matter. If a platform keeps a percentage, you must price for it. As an illustration only, if a platform kept 20 percent and you want 100 CU in hand, you would need to charge 100 / 0.80 = 125 CU. Check the real fee on the platform you use, because terms differ and change.

lessons.title: Spotting fake jobs and advance-fee scams

body.p: Online work has many honest opportunities and also many scams. Scammers target people who are eager and new. The most important rule is simple: a real employer or client pays you. You should not have to pay a stranger to get work. Learn the warning signs and trust your doubts.

list: You must pay a registration, training, uniform, equipment or 'security' fee before you start. This is an advance-fee scam.
Pay is far too high for easy work, such as a large amount for a few minutes of typing.
The recruiter contacts you first through a private chat app, uses a free email address, and avoids video or phone calls.
They send you a cheque or transfer for more than the agreed amount and ask you to forward the extra. The original payment may later fail, and you lose your own money.
They ask for your bank login, card PIN, one-time codes or a copy of identity documents before any real contract.
Spelling mistakes, pressure to act today, and a company name you cannot verify.
You are asked to receive and forward packages or money for them. This can involve you in crime.

body.p: Real clients do sometimes ask for a short paid test or a sample, and some platforms charge fees that are stated in their official terms. The difference is that legitimate costs are shown openly by the platform, you can verify them, and no one asks for secret payments or logins.

steps: Pause. Never rush because someone says the offer ends today.
Search the company name with the word 'scam' or 'reviews', and look for an official website and contacts you can verify yourself.
Check the email domain carefully and contact the company through the number on its official site, not the one in the message.
Never share passwords, PINs, one-time codes or banking logins with anyone.
Stop contact, keep screenshots, report the account on the platform and tell an adult or the local authority responsible for fraud.

body.code:
Message received: 'Congratulations! You are hired as data clerk, 300 CU per day.
Send 20 CU for your ID badge today and your bank login so we can set up pay.'

Red flags: pays too much for easy work; asks you to pay first; asks for login.
Response: do not reply with money or details. Block and report.

body.p: If you lose money, act quickly: tell your bank or mobile-money provider, report to the platform and to the relevant authority, and warn friends. Do not feel ashamed. Scammers are professionals, and reporting helps protect others.

body.tip: Before you send money or personal details to any job contact, show the message to a trusted adult. A second pair of eyes catches most scams.

lessons.title: Managing clients, deadlines, records and taxes

body.p: Winning a job is only the start. Good freelancers keep clients by being clear, reliable and calm. Repeat clients and referrals are the cheapest way to find new work. Three habits matter most: communicate early, deliver on time, and handle problems politely.

Estimate honestly, then add a buffer. Suppose a job needs 12 hours and you can give it 3 hours a day. 12 / 3 = 4 working days. Add 1 day of buffer for problems, and promise delivery in 5 days. If you also have school or other jobs, count only the hours you really have. Delivering a day early looks professional; delivering late damages trust.

body.code:
Deadline plan
Work needed        : 12 hours
Hours per day      : 3
Days of work       : 12 / 3 = 4
Buffer             : 1 day
Promise to client  : 5 working days

body.p: If something goes wrong, tell the client as soon as you know, say what you can deliver and when, and offer a solution. Do not disappear. Most clients accept honest delays but not silence.

list: Confirm requirements in writing before starting and repeat them back.
Show a draft early, so a misunderstanding costs hours, not days.
Keep to the agreed number of revisions, and politely quote for extra requests.
Stay respectful when you disagree. Keep messages short, specific and kind.
If a client keeps asking for free extra work or refuses to pay, stop, keep records, and use the platform's dispute process or other lawful steps, depending on where you live.

body.h: Records and taxes in general terms

body.p: Income from freelancing may be taxable or may need registration in your country, depending on your age and income. We cannot tell you the rules, because they differ and change. What every freelancer can do is keep good records, so that you can answer any question later. Check official government sources or ask a qualified accountant or adviser where you live.

body.code:
Simple money log (one row per payment or cost)
Date     Client     Description          In    Out   Receipt?
03 Mar   Mr Mensah  Flyer design         40    -     invoice 001
05 Mar   -          Data bundle          -     6     receipt
09 Mar   Ms Bello   CV formatting x3     24    -     invoice 002
Month total: in 64, out 6, net 58

list: Record every payment and every business cost, and keep invoices and receipts.
Put aside part of each payment so a tax bill or fee does not surprise you.
Keep records for as long as local rules say. Ask what that period is.
Keep business money separate from personal spending where you can, for example in a separate wallet or account.
Review your log monthly and compare it with your minimum rate.

body.tip: Spend 15 minutes every Friday updating your log and invoices. Small regular habits beat a big panic at the end of the year.

options: An employee of one company whose employer sets all hours, duties and pay
A self-employed person who finds their own clients, sets prices and delivers the work
Someone who works for free for every client to build up a name in the market
A person who is tied to working only for one company for their whole career

quiz.q: A student can type fast, write good English and make posters in Canva. Which first service is the best choice?
options: Offer every possible service to every kind of client so nobody is turned away
Offer advanced coding and app development, even though the student cannot do it yet
Wait until someone offers a job, then learn the needed skills after accepting it
Poster design and CV formatting for local shops and students, with a few samples

quiz.q: You have no clients. What is the most honest way to build a portfolio?
options: Make labelled practice projects and help people you know, with their permission
Copy designs from other freelancers and present them as your own client work
Invent client names and glowing reviews so the portfolio looks busy and trusted
Do nothing and wait until a client hires you, then start building samples

quiz.q: Which opening to a proposal is strongest?
options: The same 'Dear sir, I am the best' message copied and sent to every job you find
Four long paragraphs about your life story and why you started freelancing
A message that names the client's problem, links a relevant sample and suggests a next step
A promise to do any job tonight for any price the client chooses to pay

quiz.q: You need 740 CU net per month, set aside 10 percent of earnings, and can bill 60 hours a month. What is your minimum hourly rate to the nearest 0.10?
You work 40 hours a week but only 40 percent of it is billable. How many billable hours do you have?
options: 40 hours
24 hours
16 hours
10 hours

quiz.q: You estimate 12 hours at 12 CU per hour and add a 25 percent buffer. What fixed price do you quote?
options: 144 CU
180 CU
169 CU
192 CU

quiz.q: After you agree a fixed-price logo, the client asks for three extra versions not in the agreement. What is the best response?
options: Do them all for free, to avoid any conflict and keep the client happy
Refuse to speak to the client again and leave the project unfinished
Do them and quietly accept working for less than your minimum rate
Politely explain it is outside the agreed scope and quote a price for it

quiz.q: A fixed-price job paid 100 CU but took 14 hours. What was your effective hourly rate?
options: About 8.33 CU per hour
14 CU per hour
100 CU per hour
About 7.14 CU per hour

quiz.q: Which set of terms is most useful in a written agreement for a small design job?
options: Scope, price, deadline, revisions, payment dates and ownership of the work
Only the client's name and phone number, so you can reach them later
Only the price, since that is the part the client cares about most
Nothing at all, since friends who hire you will rarely disagree over money

quiz.q: A 200 CU job is paid 30 percent before starting, 40 percent at first draft and 30 percent on delivery. How much have you received after the first two payments?
options: 60 CU
140 CU
80 CU
200 CU

quiz.q: A platform keeps 20 percent of the amount you charge. To receive 100 CU yourself, what should you charge?
options: 120 CU
100 CU
125 CU
80 CU

quiz.q: A recruiter says you are hired but must first pay a 'training kit' fee. What is the best response?
options: Treat it as a likely advance-fee scam, do not pay, and report them
Pay a small amount first to test whether the recruiter is honest
Pay the fee but ask for a receipt and the contract afterwards
Ask a friend to pay the fee for you so your own money is safe

quiz.q: A chat contact offers high pay for easy tasks and asks for your bank login to 'set up payments'. What should you do?
options: Share the login because they promised high pay and easy tasks
Refuse, share nothing, keep screenshots and report the account
Share only half of the login, so they cannot use all of it
Send your ID and card PIN instead, since those are safer to give

quiz.q: A job needs 12 hours and you can work 3 hours a day. You want a 1-day buffer. What delivery time should you promise?
options: 4 working days
3 working days
5 working days
12 working days

quiz.q: Which habit best prepares a freelancer for taxes and disputes?
options: Remember payments and costs in your head, since writing them down wastes time
Delete messages after each job, to keep your phone clear and your records tidy
Assume tax rules are the same in every country, so you can copy a friend's method
Record every payment and cost, keep invoices and receipts, and check local tax rules
